widgets.name: Column
widgets.note: `textDirection` sets which side `CrossAxisAlignment.start` and `end` mean for this column only; by default the nearest `Directionality`. As in Flutter, a column keeps within the height its parent offers, and children that overflow start at its top, whatever `mainAxisAlignment`, and draw past its end

widgets.name: Row
widgets.note: `textDirection` sets the order of this row only, for example a phone number kept left to right in a right-to-left screen; by default the nearest `Directionality`. As in Flutter, a child that is not in an `Expanded` or `Flexible` has no width limit: a text wider than the row stays on one line and runs past the row's end. Put it in an `Expanded` or `Flexible` to wrap it or end it with an ellipsis. A row keeps within the width its parent offers, and children that overflow start at its start, whatever `mainAxisAlignment`, and draw past its end

widgets.name: Flex
widgets.note: `textDirection` as on `Row` and `Column`

widgets.name: Expanded
widgets.note: Takes its share of the free space whatever its content, as in Flutter: two `Expanded` children with `flex: 1` are the same width

widgets.name: Flexible
widgets.note: As in Flutter, the child gets at most its share of the free space and a smaller child keeps its own size (`fit: FlexFit.loose`, the default); `FlexFit.tight` fills the share like `Expanded`

widgets.name: Stack
widgets.note: As in Flutter, a `Positioned` child that reaches past the `Stack` makes it clip: everything past its edges is cut. A child that is not positioned never makes it clip. `clipBehavior: Clip.none` lets every child draw outside, as a badge at `top: -8` needs. A child with a key keeps its state when the children are reordered, added or removed, as in Flutter. A `Stack` whose children are all positioned takes the biggest size its parent allows, as in Flutter

widgets.name: Positioned
widgets.note: A child of the `Stack` or what a child's `build` returns, also inside a `Visibility`, as in Flutter. Its child is as wide as `left` and `right` leave it, or as `width` says; with only one of them it is as wide as its content. The same holds for `top`, `bottom` and `height`, as in Flutter. `Positioned.directional(textDirection:, start:, end:, …)` places by start and end in the direction you give; `Positioned.fromRect` and `Positioned.fromRelativeRect` (with `RelativeRect`) as in Flutter

widgets.name: PositionedDirectional
widgets.note: A `Positioned` by `start` and `end` instead of left and right, as in Flutter: they follow the nearest `Directionality`, or the app's direction, so a badge at `end: 8` sits on the right in left-to-right text and on the left in right-to-left text, and moves when the direction changes

widgets.name: Container
widgets.note: `width: double.infinity`, `height: double.infinity` and `constraints: BoxConstraints.expand()` take the whole of that side of the space the parent gives, as `SizedBox` does. `transform` and `transformAlignment` transform the whole box, as in Flutter. A `Container` with only a child is no box of its own, as in Flutter: a child that a transform moves out of it still takes taps where it is drawn. `clipBehavior` as in Flutter: by default nothing is clipped, so a rounded or circular decoration shapes the fill, border and shadow and a child that reaches the corners keeps its own; `Clip.antiAlias` (or `hardEdge`) cuts the child to the decoration's shape, and the shadow still shows

widgets.name: SizedBox
widgets.note: `double.infinity` takes the whole of that side of the space the parent gives, as in Flutter: `SizedBox(width: double.infinity)` spans a column, and `SizedBox.expand()` or `SizedBox.fromSize(size: Size.infinite)` fill both sides. As a child of a `Stack` that is not `Positioned`, it makes the `Stack` fill that side of its space too. In a `Wrap`, `width: double.infinity` makes the box as wide as the `Wrap`, on a line of its own. In a `Row` or `Column`, along its direction, where Flutter reports an error, the box takes the space the other children leave; in a scroll view, along the scrolling direction, it keeps its child's size

widgets.name: ConstrainedBox
widgets.note: Lays its child out within the limits, as in Flutter, and is laid out as `Container(constraints:)`. A size the parent sets, such as a grid cell, an `Expanded`, or the width of a stretched column or a list, takes precedence over the limits, as in Flutter. A minimum height reaches the child, which fills the box.

widgets.name: DecoratedBox
widgets.note: Paints its decoration behind its child, or over it with `position: DecorationPosition.foreground`, where touches still reach the child. It takes its child's size: no padding, not even for a border, and nothing is clipped, so the child keeps its own corners. It paints what a `Container`'s decoration paints: a colour or a linear gradient (a radial gradient shows its first colour), the top-left corner radius on all four corners, a circle (a capsule on a box that is not square), a border drawn on every side as its top side is, and the first shadow

widgets.name: Align
widgets.note: Any alignment from -1 to 1 on each axis: `Alignment(0.5, 0)` puts the child three quarters of the way to the right, and an animated alignment moves smoothly. `widthFactor` and `heightFactor` size the box as a multiple of its child, unless the room it is given is fixed (an `Expanded` share, a sized parent), which it then fills. Along a `Row`'s or a `Column`'s main axis an `Align` is as long as its child, as in Flutter: a `Column` holding a `Center` puts the centred text at the top, not in the middle of the screen. A factor on an axis where the child fills all the room it is given (a `ListView`, `SizedBox.expand()`) leaves the box filling that axis

widgets.name: Center
widgets.note: Any alignment from -1 to 1 on each axis: `Alignment(0.5, 0)` puts the child three quarters of the way to the right, and an animated alignment moves smoothly. `widthFactor` and `heightFactor` size the box as a multiple of its child, unless the room it is given is fixed (an `Expanded` share, a sized parent), which it then fills. Along a `Row`'s or a `Column`'s main axis an `Align` is as long as its child, as in Flutter: a `Column` holding a `Center` puts the centred text at the top, not in the middle of the screen. A factor on an axis where the child fills all the room it is given (a `ListView`, `SizedBox.expand()`) leaves the box filling that axis

widgets.name: Divider
widgets.note: On iPhone the table separator: one pixel in the separator grey.

widgets.name: VerticalDivider
widgets.note: On iPhone the table separator: one pixel in the separator grey.

widgets.name: Opacity
widgets.note: A child at opacity 0 still takes taps, as in Flutter

widgets.name: Visibility
widgets.note: Default flags match Flutter (hidden child is replaced and its state disposed). The full `maintain*` set is supported: with `maintainState: true` the child stays mounted and is hidden natively — pair with `maintainSize` to keep its layout slot. A hidden child takes no taps, unless `maintainInteractivity` is set

widgets.name: Offstage
widgets.note: The offstage child is unmounted (state lost) — Flutter keeps it mounted at zero size. For state-preserving show/hide, use `IndexedStack`

widgets.name: ClipRRect
widgets.note: Rounded rect clip via `Container(decoration: BoxDecoration(borderRadius: ...))`

widgets.name: ClipRSuperellipse
widgets.note: iOS squircle clip — wraps child in `ShapeDecoration(shape: RoundedSuperellipseBorder(...))`

widgets.name: ClipOval
widgets.note: Circle clip via `BoxDecoration(shape: BoxShape.circle)`

widgets.name: ClipRect
widgets.note: As large as its child, or as the room it is given when that is fixed (an `Expanded` share, a sized parent), and clips what reaches past its edges. `clipBehavior: Clip.none` draws the child unclipped

widgets.name: Wrap
widgets.note: flex-wrap. `alignment`, `runAlignment`, `spacing`, `runSpacing` and `crossAxisAlignment` work as in Flutter: runs that overflow start at the wrap's start, a child is at most the wrap's width, and what overflows a wrap in a box of fixed size draws past it

widgets.name: FractionallySizedBox
widgets.note: Sizes its child to a fraction of the space around it, placed by `alignment`. Where that space is not fixed (a `Column` that does not stretch, a `Center`), the box itself is the fraction

widgets.name: IntrinsicWidth
widgets.note: Sizes the child to its own width or height: a `Column` of buttons as wide as the widest, a `Row` as tall as its tallest child

widgets.name: IntrinsicHeight
widgets.note: Sizes the child to its own width or height: a `Column` of buttons as wide as the widest, a `Row` as tall as its tallest child

widgets.name: FittedBox
widgets.note: Lays the child out at its natural size, then scales it into the box per `fit` (every `BoxFit`) and places it by `alignment`; `clipBehavior` cuts what reaches past the box

widgets.name: ColoredBox
widgets.note: Prefer over `Container(color:…)` for simple fills

widgets.name: IgnorePointer
widgets.note: Blocks hit testing for the subtree. Decided when a pointer goes down: a drag already in progress keeps flowing when `ignoring` flips mid-gesture

widgets.name: AbsorbPointer
widgets.note: Touches in its box reach neither its child nor what is behind it; widgets around it, such as an outer `GestureDetector` or a scroll view, still get them. Decided when a pointer goes down

widgets.name: IndexedStack
widgets.note: One child visible at a time; all children stay mounted (state + scroll position preserved — the tab-switcher pattern). Sizing note: fills its parent (Flutter sizes to the largest child) — wrap in a `SizedBox` when you need an intrinsic size

widgets.name: LayoutBuilder
widgets.note: Provides parent `BoxConstraints` to the builder

widgets.name: Directionality
widgets.note: `Directionality.of(context)` works everywhere: every screen starts from the direction the platform lays the app out in, which is right-to-left only when the app declares a right-to-left language (`CFBundleLocalizations` on iOS, `android:supportsRtl` on Android). Wrap a subtree to override it: its rows, cross-axis alignment, directional padding and alignment and `TextAlign.start` follow it. Horizontal scroll views keep the app's direction. `MediaQueryData.textDirection` carries the same value

widgets.name: EdgeInsetsDirectional
widgets.note: `EdgeInsetsDirectional.fromSTEB` included; `start` and `end` follow the nearest `Directionality`; `AlignmentDirectional` is its own type, as in Flutter, and `AlignmentGeometry.resolve` gives the physical `Alignment`

widgets.name: AlignmentDirectional
widgets.note: `EdgeInsetsDirectional.fromSTEB` included; `start` and `end` follow the nearest `Directionality`; `AlignmentDirectional` is its own type, as in Flutter, and `AlignmentGeometry.resolve` gives the physical `Alignment`

widgets.name: Card
widgets.note: Without a `color`, the platform's card: Material's outlined card on Android (the surface colour with a thin edge, no shadow), white with a shadow on iOS. `elevation` left out is that default; a `color` of your own drops the edge. `clipBehavior` as in Flutter: nothing is clipped by default; use `Clip.antiAlias` when the content reaches the corners, such as an image at the top.

widgets.name: ListTile
widgets.note: Leading / title / subtitle / trailing row. On Android the title and subtitle wear Material's list item type and colours unless you style them. On Android the tile is at least 56 dp tall, 72 with a subtitle, with its content centred and 8 dp above and below the text, as in Flutter. On iPhone the subtitle is 15 pt in the secondary style, the text colour at half opacity, and the row is the 70 pt row of a plain list, 15 pt above and below the two lines. `onTap` and `onLongPress` make the row answer a press as the platform's own list rows do: the grey highlight of a table row on iPhone, the ripple of a Material list item on Android. `enabled: false` ignores them and dims the row, as in Flutter.

widgets.name: Table
widgets.note: Column-sized grid layout

widgets.name: BackdropFilter
widgets.note: Native backdrop blur (Gaussian) — `UIVisualEffectView` (iOS) / `RenderEffect` (Android)

widgets.name: ImageFiltered
widgets.note: Blurs the child's own content (Gaussian)

widgets.name: ShaderMask
widgets.note: Shows the child through a `LinearGradient` or `RadialGradient` (`createShader(bounds)`): `BlendMode.dstIn` keeps it where the gradient is opaque, `BlendMode.dstOut` where it is transparent, and the default `BlendMode.modulate` with white colours works as `dstIn`. The system draws the mask, so a child that moves inside it, such as a scrolling title, is not redrawn. The child shows only inside the mask's box

widgets.name: SnackBar
widgets.note: Shown via `ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar`; `content`, `backgroundColor`, `duration`, and `action: SnackBarAction(label:, onPressed:)`

widgets.name: RepaintBoundary
widgets.note: Captures a widget as an image, as in Flutter: give it a `GlobalKey`, then `(key.currentContext!.findRenderObject() as RenderRepaintBoundary).toImage(pixelRatio: 3)`, and `image.toByteData(format: ui.ImageByteFormat.png)` for a PNG, or `image.toJpeg(quality: 90)` for a JPEG at a quality from 0 to 100 (DartNative's own: Flutter has no JPEG there; transparent pixels come out white). Both files are encoded by the platform's own encoder, off the UI thread; on iPhone the PNG favours speed over size, so use the JPEG for a small file. `ui.Image` and `ui.ImageByteFormat` come from `import 'package:dartnative/canvas.dart' as ui;`, where Flutter code imports `dart:ui`. The image is the widget as the platform draws it, all of it, also the parts scrolled out of sight. A video, a map or a camera preview inside it is left out, as Flutter leaves out a platform view, and on Android so is a `BackdropFilter` blur. It adds no view and does not change the layout

widgets.name: Text
widgets.note: `UILabel`. A `Text` with no colour takes the platform's default text colour: the label colour on iOS; on Android the colour a `TextView` with no style has, the theme's secondary text colour. A `ListTile` title and the bar title use the primary text colour, as Material's styles do. Under a screen with a forced `Scaffold.brightness`, or in a sheet or dialog opened over it, it is the primary colour of that brightness. `textWidthBasis` works as in Flutter: a text that wraps takes the whole width it is given; `TextWidthBasis.longestLine` makes it as wide as its longest line, for a chat bubble.

widgets.name: RichText
widgets.note: `NSMutableAttributedString` — per-span font, color, weight, italic, underline, strikethrough. `const TextSpan(...)` works as in Flutter. `TextSpan.recognizer: TapGestureRecognizer` supported for tappable spans. `textWidthBasis` as on `Text`. `TextSpan` is not `const` — remove `const` from all `TextSpan(...)` calls

widgets.name: TextSpan
widgets.note: `NSMutableAttributedString` — per-span font, color, weight, italic, underline, strikethrough. `const TextSpan(...)` works as in Flutter. `TextSpan.recognizer: TapGestureRecognizer` supported for tappable spans. `textWidthBasis` as on `Text`. `TextSpan` is not `const` — remove `const` from all `TextSpan(...)` calls

widgets.name: TextField
widgets.note: `UITextField` / `UITextView`. `style.letterSpacing` spaces the field's text the way it spaces a `Text`, on both platforms. `keyboardType` opens the keyboard each `TextInputType` opens in Flutter: `TextInputType.number` is the digits-only pad, `TextInputType.numberWithOptions(decimal: true)` adds the decimal separator key, the one of the user's region (a comma in much of Europe), and `signed: true` allows a minus sign (on iPhone the numbers and punctuation keyboard, since the number pads have no minus key). `autofillHints` (the `AutofillHints` strings), `AutofillGroup` and `TextInput.finishAutofillContext()` work as in Flutter: the one-time code from Messages above the keyboard, the password manager's entries and its offer to save. On Android, `labelText` is Material's floating label: it sits in the field and moves up onto the box's edge when the field is focused. `labelText`, `helperText`, an `OutlineInputBorder` or `filled` give the field Material's box; a field with only `hintText` is Android's plain field, whose hint stays in place and clears as the user types, the kind a chat screen uses. If `InputDecoration.contentPadding` is omitted, the field uses the platform's own inset: 14 all round on iOS, and on Android the plain field's 4dp beside and 10dp above and below the text, or Material's 16dp for a Material field (override explicitly to customize). `inputFormatters` run on every edit before the keystroke is drawn, caret included: `FilteringTextInputFormatter` (`digitsOnly`, `allow`, `deny`), `LengthLimitingTextInputFormatter`, or your own `TextInputFormatter` over `TextEditingValue` / `TextSelection` `onSubmitted` fires when the user taps the keyboard's action key — the key itself is chosen by `textInputAction` (Done, Go, Search, Send, Next) — and receives the field's current text. As in Flutter, only single-line fields report a submission: in a multiline field that key inserts a newline. The key then ends the edit as in Flutter: Done (the default for a one-line field when you set no `textInputAction`; Apple's search field on iPhone keeps its Search key), Go, Search and Send close the keyboard and take the focus away, and Next moves to the following text field, on iPhone too. On the last field Next closes the keyboard, as a native form does; in Flutter, Next goes to the next widget that can take the focus, a button included, and from the last one back to the first. If your `onSubmitted` moves the focus itself, your choice wins. **The field owns its box:** `InputDecoration.border` given as an `OutlineInputBorder` (its side's colour and width, one radius), `focusedBorder`, `enabledBorder` and `disabledBorder` by Flutter's precedence, and `filled` with a `fillColor`, are drawn by the native field itself, so a decorated field is one native view: the keyboard reveals the whole box, and the focused outline follows focus. `InputBorder.none`, an `UnderlineInputBorder` and no border leave the platform's own look. A box an app draws around a field is not the field, and the keyboard keeps only the field visible, as a native Android field does. On Android, a decoration with `labelText`, `helperText`, an `OutlineInputBorder` or `filled` is drawn by Material's own text field: the label floats onto the edge when the field takes focus, the helper line sits below, and the outlined or filled box has Material's colours and its 56dp height; an explicit border side, corner radius or `fillColor` still applies, and `hintText` is the placeholder. A field with none of those is Android's plain field with its underline; `InputBorder.none` removes it. On iOS the field stays bare and `labelText`/`helperText` are not drawn. `errorBorder` is not drawn. On iPhone a field whose `OutlineInputBorder` keeps its default side is the platform's own rounded field, 34 pt with its grey bezel; `labelText` stands in for a missing `hintText` there; a bare field is the text line alone, with no inset. **Search fields:** a single-line field whose `prefixIcon` is the search icon (`Icons.search` or `CupertinoIcons.search`) is the platform's own search field. On iPhone it is Apple's search field, as tall as the one in a search bar, with its clear button while the user types; Apple draws its box and places its text there, so the decoration's border, fill and `contentPadding` do not apply. On Android a field with a label, a border or a fill shows the icon in Material's own place at the start of the box; set `prefixIconPadding` to place it yourself. `prefixIconSize` defaults to the platform's size. `clearButtonMode` adds a clear button (on Android Material's own round ✕ at the end of the box, which hides a `suffixIcon` while it shows), and `clearIconColor` tints it.

widgets.name: TextEditingController
widgets.note: `text`, `value`, `selection`, `clear()`. Typing updates the controller before `onChanged`; a selection the user makes, or a caret they move, updates `selection` and tells the listeners, without calling `onChanged`. Setting `selection` or `value` moves the caret, setting `text` keeps it where the field has it. Focusing the field from code keeps a selection the controller already has, as in Flutter

widgets.name: TextPainter
widgets.note: Drop-in replacement backed by the platform's text measurement — call `layout(maxWidth:)` then read `.size`. As in Flutter, a text that wraps is as wide as the `maxWidth` given (`textWidthBasis: TextWidthBasis.longestLine` keeps the longest line), and `minWidth` is honoured

widgets.name: RenderParagraph
widgets.note: Drop-in replacement — `layout(BoxConstraints)` + `.size`; no RenderObject tree required

widgets.name: SelectableText
widgets.note: Covered by `Text(selectable: true)` — long-press to select/copy on BOTH platforms. Plain `Text` stays `UILabel` / `TextView`; the flag swaps in a read-only `UITextView` (iOS) / read-only `EditText` (Android), so use plain `Text` when selection isn't needed. Its width is Flutter's `SelectableText`'s: a text that wraps takes the whole width it is given, or its longest line with `textWidthBasis: TextWidthBasis.longestLine`, and the box keeps a 3-point margin for the caret. A dedicated `SelectableText` class is not exported; pass the flag.

widgets.name: ListView
widgets.note: A list of `children` lays out all its items, as in Flutter. With no `padding`, a list keeps its first and last items clear of the status bar and the home indicator (or navigation bar), as Flutter's does: unless the screen's `AppBar`, a bottom bar, a `SafeArea`, an outer list, a sheet or a dialog already keeps them clear. On a `Scaffold` with `extendBody: true` the list runs behind the bottom bar, and its last item rests above the bar, as in Flutter; on iOS 26, when the tab bar minimizes on scroll or has a bottom accessory or a search tab, give the list a bottom padding of its own. Pass `padding: EdgeInsets.zero` to have none. `MediaQuery.padding` itself still reports the whole safe area

widgets.name: KeepAlive
widgets.note: Keep an item of a lazy list built while it is off screen, its `State` included: `ListView.builder`, `.separated`, `GridView.builder`, a lazy `CustomScrollView`, `FastList` and `FastGrid`. `AutomaticKeepAlive` is accepted and shows its child

widgets.name: AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin
widgets.note: Keep an item of a lazy list built while it is off screen, its `State` included: `ListView.builder`, `.separated`, `GridView.builder`, a lazy `CustomScrollView`, `FastList` and `FastGrid`. `AutomaticKeepAlive` is accepted and shows its child

widgets.name: SingleChildScrollView
widgets.note: A horizontal one in a `Column` is as tall as its content, as in Flutter, with no `SizedBox` around it. `keyboardDismissBehavior: ScrollViewKeyboardDismissBehavior.onDrag` hides the keyboard when a drag scrolls the view, as on `ListView` and `CustomScrollView`: the system's own on iPhone, the keyboard closing as the drag starts on Android. With the default `manual`, a drag that reaches the keyboard still pulls it down on iPhone

widgets.name: RefreshIndicator
widgets.note: Pull to refresh on the vertical scrollable inside it: `onRefresh`, `color`, `backgroundColor`; start a refresh from code with `GlobalKey<RefreshIndicatorState>` and `show()`. `style: RefreshStyle.pullDown` (default): the content follows the finger and a spinner shows in the band the pull opens above it (`UIRefreshControl` on iOS, a Material spinner on Android), turning once the pull passes the threshold; `color` is the spinner's colour and `backgroundColor` the band's, and left out the spinner is drawn for the screen's brightness. For content that runs under a header (a feed's tabs, the status bar), `edgeOffset` keeps the spinner in the band below it, never over the content, `displacement` is how far below that edge the content rests while the refresh runs, and `triggerDistance` how far the band opens before letting go refreshes. In this style the spinner is the platform's own, recoloured with `color`; give a `builder` and the platform's spinner stays hidden while the content still follows the finger: the builder gets the pull (phase, the band's height as `distance`, progress), through the refresh and the way back so what it draws follows the content, and draws in the band, a `PullDownIndicator` restyled or with a `child` of your own in the spinner's place, a logo or an arrow turning with the pull, riding with the content a `gap` above its edge and sliding under the header's edge as the band closes; the builder wraps the whole child, so it may keep the pull's look through the refresh and show the loading anywhere on the page, your `onRefresh` future being the loading state; `RefreshStyle.pullOver` holds the content still and draws the indicator over it: by default a video feed's: a gradient darkens the top of the screen while the pull lasts, and the line, `label` ("Pull down to refresh"), fades in under the top safe area and slides down a little with the pull, playing back when you let go, with a spinner in its place while the refresh runs, a `child` of your own there instead (an animated icon, beside the line while you pull and in its place while the refresh runs), or none with `showSpinner: false`; or give a `builder(context, child, state)` and draw your own from the state's phase, distance and progress, placing a `PullOverIndicator` where you like. `triggerDistance` is the release threshold. Works on `ListView`, `SingleChildScrollView`, `FastList`, a vertical `PageView`, the grids and `CustomScrollView`; the control sits at the top, so a horizontal or reversed scrollable has none

widgets.name: CustomScrollView
widgets.note: Lazy, as in Flutter, when its slivers are `SliverToBoxAdapter`, `SliverList` and `SliverFixedExtentList` with a count, `SliverGrid` with a fixed column count, and `SliverPadding` around them: rows are built as they near the screen, on the platform's own list. With other slivers (`SliverAppBar`, `SliverFillRemaining`, a grid sized by a maximum extent) every sliver is built. With `reverse: true` the first sliver is at the bottom, as in Flutter. `listController` counts items of the first list sliver

widgets.name: SliverFixedExtentList
widgets.note: `.builder` and `.list`; every item takes `itemExtent`

widgets.name: SliverGrid
widgets.note: `.count` and `.extent` constructors; `.extent` takes as many columns as fit its width; cells come in rows

widgets.name: SliverPadding
widgets.note: Pads the sliver as a whole, as in Flutter

widgets.name: SliverFillRemaining
widgets.note: Takes what the viewport has left after the slivers before it, as in Flutter. By default (`hasScrollBody: true`) its child is always the size of what shows of it, and the view scrolls on until it fills the screen; with `hasScrollBody: false` a taller child keeps its own height. Inside a `SliverPadding` the padding before it counts, as in Flutter. In a reversed view too, its child sits right against the slivers before it

widgets.name: SliverAppBar
widgets.note: Every named parameter of Flutter's widget is accepted. In a `NestedScrollView` header it collapses natively: `expandedHeight`, `collapsedHeight`, `pinned`, `floating`, `snap`, `bottom`, `toolbarHeight`, the title, leading and actions, `backgroundColor`, and a `FlexibleSpaceBar.background` behind the bar. In a `CustomScrollView` it is a bar at the top of the content; its collapse there and the `FlexibleSpaceBar` title are not available yet

widgets.name: GridView
widgets.note: `.count`, `.extent` and `.builder`. `GridView.builder` is lazy, as in Flutter: cells are built as they near the screen and let go once they are more than `cacheExtent` off it (250 points unless set), on the platform's own grid, the one `FastGrid` uses, so it scrolls smoothly at any `itemCount`; a cell's `State` ends off screen unless the cell asks to stay, as in `ListView.builder`. With no `padding` it keeps clear of the status bar and the home indicator as `ListView` does. With `shrinkWrap: true` or `NeverScrollableScrollPhysics` every cell is built, as in Flutter. `GridView.extent`, or a `SliverGridDelegateWithMaxCrossAxisExtent`, takes as many columns as fit cells no wider than `maxCrossAxisExtent`, so a wider screen or a rotation gets more columns. A cell's content fills the cell, as in Flutter: a `Card` in a cell is as tall as the cell, and a `Container` or `SizedBox` with a height of its own takes the cell's. `showScrollBar: true` shows the scroll indicator, on a horizontal grid too, and a change on a rebuild applies

widgets.name: ScrollController
widgets.note: On `ListView`, `GridView`, `SingleChildScrollView` and `CustomScrollView`: `offset`, `position.pixels` and `position.maxScrollExtent` follow the scroll along the view's axis, and `position.maxScrollExtent` and `position.viewportDimension` are known once the view is laid out, before any scroll, as in Flutter. `jumpTo` and `animateTo` move the view along it, so a horizontal `ListView`, `GridView` or `SingleChildScrollView` reads and moves sideways. A rebuild that gives the view another controller, a first one or none is followed. On a reversed list, offset 0 is the list's start, its bottom, as in Flutter: `jumpTo(0)` shows the newest message of a chat. `position.isScrollingNotifier` tells when the view starts and stops scrolling, and `position.userScrollDirection` the way the user scrolls it, as in Flutter

widgets.name: NotificationListener
widgets.note: Hears the notifications that bubble up from below, as in Flutter: return `true` from `onNotification` to stop one there. `Notification.dispatch(context)` sends your own. `ListView`, `GridView`, `SingleChildScrollView`, `CustomScrollView`, `FastList`, `FastGrid` and `MasonryFastGrid` send Flutter's scroll notifications in Flutter's order: `ScrollStartNotification`, `UserScrollNotification`, `ScrollUpdateNotification`, `ScrollEndNotification`, each with its `metrics` (`pixels`, `maxScrollExtent`, `extentAfter` and the rest) and its `depth`. A drag's notifications carry `dragDetails` with the finger's movement, not its position. A notification goes up the screen it was sent on: pushed screens, sheets and dialogs each have their own. `OverscrollNotification`, and scroll notifications from `PageView`, `NestedScrollView` and `TabBarView`, are not sent yet, and a list inside one of those three still reports a `depth` of 0 above it

widgets.name: PageView
widgets.note: `PageView`, `.builder`, `.custom` and `PageController`; each swipe settles on one page on the platform's own paging. `PageController.page` is the page the view rests on before the first swipe. A page is always the whole viewport (`viewportFraction` other than 1 is not supported)

widgets.name: NestedScrollView
widgets.note: Flutter's API: `headerSliverBuilder`, `body`, `floatHeaderSlivers`, `NestedScrollViewState` through a `GlobalKey`, `sliverOverlapAbsorberHandleFor`, `SliverOverlapAbsorber` and `SliverOverlapInjector`. The header (a `SliverAppBar`) sits over the body's top and its height follows the body's scroll natively: it shrinks away as the body scrolls, comes back when the content returns (at once when `floating`), keeps its collapsed height when `pinned`, and `snap` animates it open or shut when a drag ends, moving the content with it. The header always floats over the content; `controller`, `physics` and the other scroll-view knobs are accepted and not honoured yet; only a `SliverAppBar` renders among the header slivers

widgets.name: ReorderableListView
widgets.note: Flutter's API on the platform's own reordering: the list's own drag on iOS, the recycler's touch helper on Android, each with its auto-scroll at the edges. `children` (every item keyed) and `.builder`; `onReorder` in Flutter's index convention. A long press lifts a row by default; with `buildDefaultDragHandles: false` a `ReorderableDragStartListener` starts the drag on Android, and on iOS each row shows the platform's reorder grabber at its trailing edge, which starts the drag. `FastList` offers the same through `onReorder`. Every named parameter of Flutter's widget is accepted, so Flutter code compiles unchanged; not honoured yet: `header`/`footer`, `proxyDecorator`, `onReorderStart`/`End`, `scrollController`, `shrinkWrap`, `cacheExtent` and the other scroll-view knobs, a horizontal list.

widgets.name: FastList
widgets.note: `UICollectionView` with cell recycling | `RecyclerView`

widgets.name: FastGrid
widgets.note: `UICollectionView` with cell recycling | `RecyclerView`

widgets.name: MasonryFastGrid
widgets.note: Staggered Pinterest-style grid; heights from `itemHeightBuilder`. `UICollectionView` with a custom staggered layout | `RecyclerView` (`StaggeredGridLayoutManager`)

widgets.name: Scaffold
widgets.note: `backgroundColor` is the route's colour: on iOS 26 a push draws both screens as rounded cards over a backdrop painted with it, so a page colour painted deeper in the body than its root flashes the white default at the corners (a plain colour box at the body's root is read as the page) — see [The screen's background belongs on the Scaffold](#the-screens-background-belongs-on-the-scaffold). `brightness` declares the screen's light/dark trait (inherited by the body, bottom bars and keyboards, by the bar's title and items over the screen, by the defaults computed in Dart such as a card's surface or a list item's subtitle, and by a sheet or dialog opened from the screen; `MediaQuery.of(context).platformBrightness` reports it under the scaffold; applies from the first build). Declare it on dark-styled screens: system effects like the iOS 26 scroll-edge fades render in the trait, so a dark-by-colors screen on a light-mode device gets white flashes without it. `bottomAccessory` — any-widget strip above the bottom bar (iOS 26 tabbed pattern → native `UITabAccessory`, slides inline on minimize; composed elsewhere) — see [Bottom accessory](#bottom-accessory-scaffoldbottomaccessory-ios-26) Without a colour the screen is the platform's own page: the system background on iPhone, white in light and black in dark, and the theme's surface on Android. `ios: ScaffoldIOSConfig(scrollEdgeEffectStyle: ScrollEdgeEffectStyle.soft)` sets how the content of the screen's lists and scroll views fades out under its bars on iOS 26 and later: `soft` is the look of iOS 26, `hard` a hard edge with a line, and the default, `automatic`, is the system's choice, which from iOS 27 is the hard edge under a bar with a title. It shows where content runs under a bar: a clear or frosted `AppBar` with `extendBodyBehindAppBar`, and the tab bar with `extendBody`. A screen without an `AppBar` shows no fade under the status bar on iOS 26, whatever the style, as an iOS 26 screen without a bar. On iOS 27, an app built with the iOS 27 SDK gets the system's fade under the status bar on every screen, and the style applies there too; an app built with the iOS 26 SDK gets none there, as any app. Ignored on Android.

widgets.name: AppBar
widgets.note: `automaticallyImplyLeading` (default `true`) auto-shows back button when screen can pop. `leading`, `title`, and `actions` all accept **arbitrary widgets** (`actions` takes several — each its own glass capsule on iOS 26) — see [Custom widgets in AppBar.title and AppBar.actions](#custom-widgets-in-appbartitle-and-appbaractions). Title placement and spacing: [`centerTitle`](#appbarcentertitle) and [`titleSpacing`](#appbartitlespacing); trailing-group padding: [`actionsPadding`](#appbaractionspadding) — each has its own section below. `subtitle` renders a secondary line under the title. `largeTitle` renders a large title under the bar that **collapses natively on scroll** into the bar title (`largeTitleSize` picks the Android M3 variant: medium/large flexible) — see [Large title & the see-through bar](#large-title--the-see-through-bar-ios-26). iOS 26 bar surfaces: a **translucent `backgroundColor`** (alpha < 1) = frosted glass (content faintly visible behind); **no `backgroundColor`** = a fully clear bar where content stays visible scrolling beneath, kept legible by the system scroll-edge blur ramp. On Android, **no `backgroundColor`** = the bar takes the screen's colour (`Scaffold.backgroundColor`) and a title and back arrow with no colour of their own turn white or black to stay readable against it. `searchBar` makes the bar region the search pill itself (the `SearchBar` row below); `title` is skipped when set — the pill owns the region. `actionsGlassBackground: false` (iOS 26) removes the glass capsule behind a self-designed action widget (an avatar circle keeps just its circle). On iOS 26, a bar using only plain native features is hosted on the **system navigation bar** and its buttons **morph between screens** — see [Morphing bar buttons](#morphing-bar-buttons-ios-26-appbarios) (`ios: AppBarIOSConfig(systemBar:)` selects the host explicitly) On Android the bar is Material's 64dp top app bar with a 22sp regular title; `toolbarHeight` still sets your own. `bottom` places a widget under the toolbar, a `TabBar` normally; it shares the bar's surface and the body starts below it.

widgets.name: BackButton
widgets.note: **Semantic back preset** for `AppBar.leading` — see details below. `leading` also accepts any other widget (e.g. a `Button`), which replaces the auto back button

widgets.name: BarButtonItem
widgets.note: Convenience trailing action for `AppBar.actions` — text (`title`), SF Symbol (`icon`, iOS) or font glyph (`fontIcon`, both platforms); iOS 26 Liquid Glass capsule via default `actionsGlassBackground`. With `menu: [MenuAction(...)]` the tap shows a **native anchored menu** (capsule→UIMenu morph on iOS 26; M3 popup on Android) — see [Native menus on a bar action](#native-menus-on-a-bar-action-barbuttonitemmenu)

widgets.name: App
widgets.note: Deprecated aliases: `MaterialApp`, `CupertinoApp`. `builder:` puts a layer above every screen, as Flutter's `builder` (`WidgetsApp.builder`) does: what it lays beside `child` — a performance meter, a debug badge — stays in place while screens push and pop. `child` stands for your screens, which show through the layer, and for the app's `Overlay`, whose entries it holds; touches that miss the layer's own widgets reach the screen below, and the layer sees your `theme` and `MediaQuery`. Unlike Flutter, what the builder wraps around `child` (a Theme, padding, a banner in a Column) does not reach the screens: lay your widgets beside it in a `Stack`. Views the platform presents itself (system sheets, alerts, pickers) cover the layer, and so do dialogs and bottom sheets on Android.

widgets.name: PageRoute
widgets.note: Accepts `transition` and `duration` parameters. Deprecated alias: `MaterialPageRoute`

widgets.name: BottomNavigationBar
widgets.note: `UITabBar` — font glyph rendered directly on both platforms; no SF Symbol mapping needed. iOS 26: renders as the floating Liquid Glass pill — `backgroundColor` is ignored there and the bar manages its own home-indicator offset; pair with `Scaffold(extendBody: ...)` so content scrolls behind it — the system fade under the pill is applied automatically (declare `Scaffold.brightness` on dark screens; the fade renders in the trait). `scrollBehavior: TabBarScrollBehavior.minimizeOnScrollDown` minimizes the pill on scroll (real `UITabBarController` lowering — see [Minimize on scroll](#minimize-on-scroll-scrollbehavior-ios-26)); `BottomNavigationBarItem.search()` = the system search pill; item `subtitle`/`enabled`/`activeIcon` supported

widgets.name: TabBar
widgets.note: Flutter's API: `TabBar` (and `.secondary`) under the app bar (`AppBar.bottom`) or on its own, `Tab` with text, an icon or both, `TabBarView`, `TabController` and `DefaultTabController`. The bar is a native strip in the Material shape on both platforms (drawn by the framework on iOS, Material's own tab layout on Android); the pages swipe on the platform's paging, and the indicator follows a swipe as it happens. A tap animates to the page; `isScrollable`, `indicatorColor`, `indicatorWeight`, `labelColor`, `unselectedLabelColor`, `dividerColor`, `dividerHeight`, the label's font size and `onTap` are honoured; every other named parameter is accepted, so Flutter code compiles unchanged (`indicator`, `indicatorSize`, `padding`, `labelPadding`, `overlayColor`, `tabAlignment` and the other style knobs have no effect yet)

widgets.name: TabBarView
widgets.note: Flutter's API: `TabBar` (and `.secondary`) under the app bar (`AppBar.bottom`) or on its own, `Tab` with text, an icon or both, `TabBarView`, `TabController` and `DefaultTabController`. The bar is a native strip in the Material shape on both platforms (drawn by the framework on iOS, Material's own tab layout on Android); the pages swipe on the platform's paging, and the indicator follows a swipe as it happens. A tap animates to the page; `isScrollable`, `indicatorColor`, `indicatorWeight`, `labelColor`, `unselectedLabelColor`, `dividerColor`, `dividerHeight`, the label's font size and `onTap` are honoured; every other named parameter is accepted, so Flutter code compiles unchanged (`indicator`, `indicatorSize`, `padding`, `labelPadding`, `overlayColor`, `tabAlignment` and the other style knobs have no effect yet)

widgets.name: SegmentedControl
widgets.note: `UISegmentedControl` (iOS); Material's segmented buttons on Android, each segment as wide as the widest, as Jetpack Compose's segmented button lays them out; the control sizes to its segments unless it is given a width.

widgets.name: SegmentedButton
widgets.note: Flutter's API on the same native controls: a `label` and an `icon` per segment, `selected`, `onSelectionChanged`, `enabled`, `showSelectedIcon`, `selectedIcon`, `expandedInsets` and `style`. On Android each segment shows its icon beside its label, and the selected one a check mark in place of its icon. On iPhone a segment shows its label, or its icon when it has no label: the system's segmented control holds a title or an image in a segment, not both. If your design needs an icon and a label together on iPhone too, build your own segmented control from `Row`, `Icon`, `Text` and `GestureDetector`, as you would in Flutter. It sizes to its segments; give it a width with a `SizedBox`, or fill the row with `expandedInsets`, and the segments share it equally. One segment is selected at a time. `SegmentedButton.styleFrom` sets the colours of the segments and their labels, selected or not, the icons' colour, the label's size and weight, and on Android the outline (`side`); a disabled segment keeps the platform's disabled look

widgets.name: ButtonSegment
widgets.note: Flutter's API on the same native controls: a `label` and an `icon` per segment, `selected`, `onSelectionChanged`, `enabled`, `showSelectedIcon`, `selectedIcon`, `expandedInsets` and `style`. On Android each segment shows its icon beside its label, and the selected one a check mark in place of its icon. On iPhone a segment shows its label, or its icon when it has no label: the system's segmented control holds a title or an image in a segment, not both. If your design needs an icon and a label together on iPhone too, build your own segmented control from `Row`, `Icon`, `Text` and `GestureDetector`, as you would in Flutter. It sizes to its segments; give it a width with a `SizedBox`, or fill the row with `expandedInsets`, and the segments share it equally. One segment is selected at a time. `SegmentedButton.styleFrom` sets the colours of the segments and their labels, selected or not, the icons' colour, the label's size and weight, and on Android the outline (`side`); a disabled segment keeps the platform's disabled look

widgets.name: Drawer
widgets.note:
`Scaffold.drawer` — an opinionated slide drawer, no scrim. `drawerStyle` picks the reveal:
• **`DrawerStyle.push`** (default) — drawer and screen move **together** as one flat plane: the screen slides aside while the panel slides in from behind it, no shadow, no depth (Gmail / Spotify).
• **`DrawerStyle.slideOver`** — the drawer is a **static layer underneath, it never moves**; the screen lifts and slides over it as a floating card with an edge shadow and corners that round in as it travels (X / Twitter). Tune via `Scaffold.slideOverStyle` — `SlideOverStyle(shadow:, corner: straight/rounded, radius:)` — ignored under `push`.
Swipe to open (`drawerEnableOpenDragGesture`) or `Scaffold.of(context).openDrawer()`; tap the moved content or swipe back to close. `onDrawerChanged` fires on open/close; `Drawer.width` sets the panel width. **iOS 26, the app's first screen: a native drawer.** The panel lies behind the app's navigation, and the drawer slides the whole screen aside with its navigation bar and tab bar, as a UIKit app with a drawer does, so the AppBar stays on the system bar and its buttons morph on every push and pop. Same styles, gestures and callbacks; nothing to change in the app. Android tip: if the screen colors the system navigation-bar strip (bottom-bar screens), set it transparent while the drawer is open via `onDrawerChanged` — otherwise it draws over the sliding card's shadow. A manual AppBar hamburger wraps the button in a `Builder` so `Scaffold.of(context)` resolves below the drawer. `GlobalKey` is not supported — drive the drawer via `Scaffold.of(context)`, or use `SliderMenuContainer` directly for key-driven control. **Release feel is native per platform:** iOS follows Apple's projection rule, Android the Material flick rule; `SliderMenuContainer.settleCurve` shapes the settle, and a new drag catches a still-moving panel.

widgets.note:

widgets.name: FloatingActionButton
widgets.note: Circular `UIButton` (iOS) — `child` font glyph rendered directly on both platforms

widgets.name: BottomSheet
widgets.note: Content-sized bottom sheet hosting a native widget tree: the system sheet on iOS 16 and later, floating in from the edges on iOS 26, and Material's `BottomSheetDialog` on Android, with the dim, tap-outside and drag dismiss of each. Rides the keyboard natively: the card stays glued above it through open/close and rotation, and its height caps to the available space (content clips rather than pushing off-screen) A `PopScope` inside works as it does on a screen: `canPop: false` keeps it up against the swipe, the scrim tap and the system back, and `onPopInvokedWithResult` hears every attempt and every close, with the result passed to `Navigator.pop`, before the Future completes.

widgets.name: SheetDetent
widgets.note: Native detent sheet — `UISheetPresentationController` (iOS 15+): `medium`/`large`/`adaptive`/`fitContent`, native spring physics, swipe-to-dismiss, the grabber on `showDragHandle: true`. `fitContent` sizes to the measured content height, floating in from the edges on iOS 26 as the platform's partial sheets do (iOS 15 presents it as a bottom overlay). On Android every detent is Material's modal bottom sheet: `fitContent` sized to its content, `medium`/`adaptive` resting at half height (adaptive drags to full and stays there when its content changes; `medium` stays at half, and a list inside it scrolls; a `large` sheet let go lower returns to full), `large` at full height below the status bar, the content laid out at the sheet's height. A list or a `SingleChildScrollView` inside works with the sheet, as on iOS: dragging up grows an adaptive sheet before the content scrolls, and dragging down at the content's top shrinks it or, pulled far or fast, closes it. A `SheetHeader` lowers by default to real bar items on the sheet's own navigation bar (`systemBar: false` composes glass buttons instead): centred title, system close, up to two trailing actions. Adjacent actions share one Liquid Glass capsule; a `SizedBox(width:)` between them splits them, as in `AppBar.actions`. `SheetHeaderController.update` re-declares a live header as sheet state changes. It works the same whether the header sits on the sheet's own bar or is drawn by the framework, which is what Android and `fitContent` sheets on iOS 15 get. Content is padded below the bar automatically. Without `systemBar` the header renders as composed glass buttons. A `PopScope` inside works as it does on a screen: `canPop: false` keeps it up against the swipe, the scrim tap and the system back, and `onPopInvokedWithResult` hears every attempt and every close, with the result passed to `Navigator.pop`, before the Future completes. Opened from inside a sheet, it appears on top of the sheet.

widgets.note: Native detent sheet — `UISheetPresentationController` (iOS 15+): `medium`/`large`/`adaptive`/`fitContent`, native spring physics, swipe-to-dismiss, the grabber on `showDragHandle: true`. `fitContent` sizes to the measured content height, floating in from the edges on iOS 26 as the platform's partial sheets do (iOS 15 presents it as a bottom overlay). widgets.name: Dialog
widgets.note: Imperative `showAlert()` → `UIAlertController`

widgets.name: AlertDialog
widgets.note: Imperative `showAlert()` → `UIAlertController`

widgets.name: Overlay
widgets.note: Widgets above every screen, as in Flutter: `Overlay.of(context).insert(OverlayEntry(builder: ...))`, `insertAll`, `remove()`, `markNeedsBuild()`, `opaque` and `maintainState`. Every app has an overlay above all its screens, with or without an `App`; its entries cover the app bar, stay in place while screens push and pop (a flash can outlive the page that started it, a toast stays while pages change), and sit under what `App.builder` lays beside its `child`. Touches that land on nothing in an entry reach the screen below; wrap an entry that only shows something in `IgnorePointer`. Bottom sheets cover the overlay (on iPhone `showModalBottomSheet` is the system sheet), as do alerts and pickers the platform presents, and on Android dialogs, which are windows of their own there

widgets.name: OverlayEntry
widgets.note: Widgets above every screen, as in Flutter: `Overlay.of(context).insert(OverlayEntry(builder: ...))`, `insertAll`, `remove()`, `markNeedsBuild()`, `opaque` and `maintainState`. Every app has an overlay above all its screens, with or without an `App`; its entries cover the app bar, stay in place while screens push and pop (a flash can outlive the page that started it, a toast stays while pages change), and sit under what `App.builder` lays beside its `child`. Touches that land on nothing in an entry reach the screen below; wrap an entry that only shows something in `IgnorePointer`. Bottom sheets cover the overlay (on iPhone `showModalBottomSheet` is the system sheet), as do alerts and pickers the platform presents, and on Android dialogs, which are windows of their own there

widgets.name: ElevatedButton
widgets.note: A `Button(variant: ButtonVariant.elevated)`: on Android Material's elevated button, the light surface colour with the label in the theme colour and a soft shadow, as in Flutter; on iPhone a filled button

widgets.name: TextButton
widgets.note: A `Button(variant: ButtonVariant.plain)`

widgets.name: OutlinedButton
widgets.note: A `Button(variant: ButtonVariant.bordered)`

widgets.name: FilledButton
widgets.note: A `Button(variant: ButtonVariant.filled)`, or `tinted` for `.tonal`

widgets.name: IconButton
widgets.note: 48×48 minimum hit target (Flutter `kMinInteractiveDimension` parity); `tooltip` names the button, as `Tooltip` does. VoiceOver and TalkBack read it as a button, named by its `tooltip` or its icon's `semanticLabel`, and dimmed without `onPressed`. On Android a press draws the platform's ripple, the circle a toolbar's icons draw under the finger

widgets.name: Tooltip
widgets.note: A text that names its child, on the platform's own tooltip: `message`, or `richMessage` shown as plain text, and `excludeFromSemantics`. On Android (8 and later) the system tooltip shows on a long-press, and when a mouse pointer rests on the child. On iPhone and iPad the system tooltip shows when a trackpad or mouse pointer rests on the child; a long-press on the touch screen shows nothing, as in iOS apps, except with an accessibility text size, where it shows the text enlarged, as the system bars do. VoiceOver and TalkBack read the text: as the child's name when it shows no text of its own, such as an icon, and after its text otherwise. If your design needs a bubble on every long-press on iPhone too, build your own from `GestureDetector` and a `Stack`, as you would in Flutter

widgets.name: Semantics
widgets.note: Describes its child to VoiceOver and TalkBack, as in Flutter: `label`, `value`, `hint`, `button`, `header`, `image`, `selected`, `enabled`, `excludeSemantics`, `onTap`, `onLongPress`, `onTapHint` and `onLongPressHint`, and `link` on iPhone. The child becomes one element, read as its label followed by the text it shows (unless `excludeSemantics`), then its value and hint; text that changes inside it is read as it is now. A double tap runs `onTap`, or taps the child, so a `GestureDetector` inside works as it does for a finger. `onLongPressHint` names the long press: on iPhone an action in VoiceOver's actions list, on Android TalkBack's "double-tap and hold to …". `onTapHint` is TalkBack's "double-tap to …"; VoiceOver has no such hint

widgets.name: MergeSemantics
widgets.note: Reads its child as one element: the text and the roles of everything in it, so a row of a label and a switch is one stop that reads the switch's state, and a double tap toggles the switch

widgets.name: ExcludeSemantics
widgets.note: Hides its child from VoiceOver and TalkBack, for a decoration or text another element already reads; `excluding: false` shows it

widgets.name: NativeButton
widgets.note: `UIButton.Configuration` — filled, tinted, gray, bordered, plain. For new DN code, prefer `Button` directly.

widgets.name: InteractiveViewer
widgets.note: Pinch to zoom and drag to pan a child, run natively with no work in Dart while the fingers move: on iPhone a scroll view that zooms, with the system's bounce; on Android a zoom container with Android's fling. The viewer fills its space and the child is laid out at the viewer's size; zoomed out, the child stays centred. `minScale`, `maxScale`, `panEnabled`, `scaleEnabled`, `boundaryMargin`, `clipBehavior`.

widgets.name: GestureDetector
widgets.note: The full gesture surface, all wired to native recognizers: taps (`onTap`, `onDoubleTap`, `onLongPress`, `onTapDown`, `onTapUp`, `onTapCancel`), pan (`onPanStart/Update/End`), axis-locked drags (`onHorizontalDragStart/Update/End`, `onVerticalDragStart/Update/End`) and pinch (`onScaleStart/Update/End` — focal point and scale factor; the end velocity is how fast the scale was changing as the fingers lifted). Drag and tap details carry both `globalPosition` and `localPosition`, so scrubbers, trim handles and pinch-zoom UIs are all buildable in Dart. The tap callbacks come in Flutter's order and with its timing: `onTapDown` as the finger lands when nothing else could take the touch, and after 100 ms (or with the tap, for a quick one) inside a scroll view or beside another gesture, so a quick swipe over a list reports no tap at all; then `onTapUp` and `onTap` when it lifts, or `onTapCancel` instead when the press moves away, a scroll or a drag takes it, or it becomes a long press (before `onLongPress` runs); never `onTapCancel` after a tap. With `onDoubleTap` as well, `onTap` waits for the double-tap time, as in Flutter: a single tap runs it once no second tap can follow, and a double tap runs only `onDoubleTap` (and `onTapCancel` when `onTapDown` already ran). Each callback runs as the latest build has it, and a press carries on when a callback rebuilds the child as another widget, such as an `Opacity` or a `Transform.scale` around it while it is pressed. Of nested detectors the innermost takes the tap, and the outer ones get `onTapDown` and `onTapCancel`, as in Flutter. Unlike Flutter, a `GestureDetector` around an `IgnorePointer` still takes taps on its area: put the `IgnorePointer` around the detector to switch its taps off. A detector around a platform control (a text field, a button, a switch, a check box, a radio, a slider) leaves the control's touches to the control. A tap is silent on Android, as Flutter's `GestureDetector` is; `InkWell`, `ListTile` and `IconButton` play the system click sound. A double tap with VoiceOver or TalkBack runs `onTapDown`, `onTapUp` and `onTap`. `HitTestBehavior.translucent` works as in Flutter: where the detector's child draws nothing under the finger, the widgets behind it are reached too, and a tap or a long press goes to the frontmost one that handles it. A drag or a scroll behind a translucent detector is not reached

widgets.name: Listener
widgets.note: Reports every touch on its box: `onPointerDown`, `onPointerMove` (with `delta`), `onPointerUp` and `onPointerCancel`, with `position` on the screen, `localPosition` in the box and a `pointer` number for each finger. It keeps reporting while a scroll view or a detector takes the touch, and takes touches anywhere in its box, as `GestureDetector` does. On Android, a scroll view that contains it and takes over the drag ends its touch with `onPointerCancel`

widgets.name: InkWell
widgets.note: `onTap`, `onDoubleTap`, `onLongPress`, `onTapDown`, `onTapUp`, `onTapCancel`, with the platform's press feedback: the ripple of a Material list item on Android, in `splashColor` when set, and the grey highlight of a table row on iPhone, in `highlightColor` when set. A transparent colour turns that platform's feedback off; `borderRadius` rounds it. Without a callback it draws no feedback, as in Flutter

widgets.name: Checkbox
widgets.note: `UIButton` + SF Symbols; tristate supported

widgets.name: DropdownButton
widgets.note: The platform's own picker for one of a few values, in place: on iPhone a button showing the current item that opens the system menu anchored to it, the current item checked; on Android Material's outlined exposed dropdown menu, as wide as its widest item, `hint` inside the box while there is no `value`, never on its edge, as in Flutter. `value`, `items` (`DropdownMenuItem(value:, child: Text(...))`), `onChanged`, `hint`, `isExpanded`, `style`. It keeps showing `value` until a rebuild changes it, as in Flutter.

widgets.name: Switch
widgets.note: `UISwitch` on iPhone, Google's Material 3 switch on Android — nothing to turn on. The four colour parameters work on both. `android: AndroidSwitchStyle(checkIcon: true)` adds the tick mark inside the knob

widgets.name: CupertinoSwitch
widgets.note: `UISwitch` on iPhone, Google's Material 3 switch on Android — nothing to turn on. The four colour parameters work on both. `android: AndroidSwitchStyle(checkIcon: true)` adds the tick mark inside the knob

widgets.name: Slider
widgets.note: `UISlider` on iPhone, Google's Material 3 slider on Android — a slim upright handle with a gap either side and a dot at the end. Size it with `android: AndroidSliderStyle(...)`: `trackHeight`, `thumbWidth`, `thumbHeight`, `thumbTrackGap`, `stopIndicatorSize`, `trackCornerSize` (all in dp; set the last three to 0 for a plain bar). Colors resolve Flutter's way: the widget's `activeColor`/`inactiveColor`/`thumbColor` win, else the ambient `SliderTheme(data: SliderThemeData(...))` supplies `activeTrackColor`/`inactiveTrackColor`/`thumbColor` (reactive — sliders restyle when the theme changes). Slider geometry stays native: `SliderThemeData`'s shape classes compile for source compatibility but the track and thumb shapes are the platform's own (`android:` is the geometry knob)

widgets.name: CupertinoSlider
widgets.note: `UISlider` on iPhone, Google's Material 3 slider on Android — a slim upright handle with a gap either side and a dot at the end. Size it with `android: AndroidSliderStyle(...)`: `trackHeight`, `thumbWidth`, `thumbHeight`, `thumbTrackGap`, `stopIndicatorSize`, `trackCornerSize` (all in dp; set the last three to 0 for a plain bar). Colors resolve Flutter's way: the widget's `activeColor`/`inactiveColor`/`thumbColor` win, else the ambient `SliderTheme(data: SliderThemeData(...))` supplies `activeTrackColor`/`inactiveTrackColor`/`thumbColor` (reactive — sliders restyle when the theme changes). Slider geometry stays native: `SliderThemeData`'s shape classes compile for source compatibility but the track and thumb shapes are the platform's own (`android:` is the geometry knob)

widgets.name: CircularProgressIndicator
widgets.note: `UIActivityIndicatorView` on iPhone. On Android, `android: AndroidProgressIndicatorStyle(wavy: true)` gives Google's wavy spinner Without a colour it is the system's grey spinner.

widgets.name: LinearProgressIndicator
widgets.note: `UIProgressView` on iPhone, Google's Material 3 bar on Android (rounded ends, a gap before the dot at the end). `value` 0.0–1.0, or `null` while you don't know how long it takes: a segment slides along the bar on iPhone, Material's moving bar on Android. `android: AndroidProgressIndicatorStyle(wavy: true)` for the wave. Without colours it is the system's blue bar on the system's grey track.

widgets.name: Dismissible
widgets.note: Flutter's widget: drag the child away and `background` shows in the space it leaves (`secondaryBackground`, when set, for a drag towards the start or up). Released past its threshold (40% of its width by default, `dismissThresholds` per direction) or flung, it slides off; `confirmDismiss` can still keep it, and it slides back. Then it closes up over `resizeDuration` and `onDismissed` is called: remove the item there. `direction`, `movementDuration`, `crossAxisEndOffset`, `onUpdate`, `onResize` and `behavior` work as in Flutter. It works in a `ListView`, a `FastList` or anywhere else; give it a key that names the item, not its position

widgets.name: Clipboard
widgets.note: Flutter's call shapes: `Clipboard.setData(ClipboardData(text: ...))` writes, `Clipboard.getData(Clipboard.kTextPlain)` reads (returns `null` when the clipboard holds no text; plain text is the only format). On iPhone, reading the clipboard from code makes the system show the user a short notice — for example "YourApp pasted from Safari" — and it may first ask their permission; the clipboard can hold private data like passwords, so no app can read it silently. Read when the user asked to paste, not in the background.

widgets.name: DynamicColor
widgets.note: `DynamicColor.colorScheme(brightness:)` builds the M3 `ColorScheme` from the device's wallpaper-derived palette (Android 12+); `DynamicColor.corePalette()` exposes the raw five tonal palettes. Returns `null` where there's no device palette (iOS, Android < 12) — theme from your own seed: `scheme ?? fallback`.

widgets.name: CircleAvatar
widgets.note: `Container` + `BoxDecoration(shape: BoxShape.circle)`; `backgroundImage` takes an image provider (`NetworkImage`, `AssetImage`), cropped to the circle

widgets.name: FocusNode
widgets.note: Real platform focus. `nextFocus()` and `previousFocus()` move the focus to the next or the previous text field, as the keyboard's Next does: only text fields take it, and after the last one the keyboard closes. In Flutter they also stop at buttons and go from the last back to the first

widgets.name: Focus
widgets.note: Has focus while a field inside it has: `onFocusChange` hears each change and `focusNode` follows it. Unfocusing that node takes focus from the field.

widgets.name: FocusScope
widgets.note: `FocusScope.of(context).unfocus()` takes focus from the field that has it and drops the keyboard. `FocusScope.of(context).nextFocus()` and `previousFocus()` move it as on a `FocusNode`.

widgets.name: FocusScopeNode
widgets.note: `FocusScope.of(context).unfocus()` takes focus from the field that has it and drops the keyboard. `FocusScope.of(context).nextFocus()` and `previousFocus()` move it as on a `FocusNode`.

widgets.name: FocusManager
widgets.note: `FocusManager.instance.primaryFocus` is the node of the field that has focus; `primaryFocus?.unfocus()` drops the keyboard.

widgets.name: BoxDecoration
widgets.note: color, borderRadius, border, gradient, shadows

widgets.name: BoxShadow
widgets.note: As in Flutter: a shadow with no blur, the default, has hard edges; `spreadRadius` grows the shadow and keeps the box's corners; a box with no colour still casts the shadow of its whole shape; under an `Opacity` the whole shadow fades with the box

widgets.name: LinearGradient
widgets.note: `createShader(rect)` gives the shader for a `ShaderMask` or `Paint.shader`

widgets.name: RadialGradient
widgets.note: `createShader(rect)`, as for `LinearGradient`

widgets.name: StadiumBorder
widgets.note: Pill shape

widgets.name: RoundedSuperellipseBorder
widgets.note: iOS squircle (`CALayer.cornerCurve = .continuous`). Use directly via `ShapeDecoration` or via `ClipRSuperellipse`
